title: Why did Bitcoin add Schnorr signatures?
dek: BIP 340 gives Bitcoin a compact, precisely specified signature scheme. Its structure supports batch verification and protocols that combine several signers into one signature.

blocks.text: Bitcoin already had ECDSA signatures. BIP 340 standardizes Schnorr signatures over the same curve, secp256k1. Its authors point to security proofs under established assumptions and non-malleability: a third party cannot turn a valid signature into a different valid signature for the same key and message under those assumptions.

The format also has practical benefits: fixed-size signatures, smaller public keys and efficient verification of many signatures together. Schnorr’s linear structure supports protocols in which several people cooperate to produce one signature. BIP 340 supplies the signature scheme; a protocol such as MuSig2 supplies the coordination between signers.

The signer uses a secret key and a message to produce a signature. The verifier receives the public key, the message and that signature, and checks their mathematical relationship. The secret key stays with the signer. The overview below shows that handoff; the interactive example then follows the verifier using published test vectors.

figure.title: From signing to verification
figure.caption: The signing handoff is schematic; this page does not sign. Below it, published vector 1 enters the verifier: an x-only public key, a message and a signature. No secret key enters the verifier.

blocks.text: The verifier’s inputs have fixed shapes. The public key is exactly 32 bytes. The signature is exactly 64 bytes. The message is a byte array of any length, including none at all.

Those sizes were deliberate choices. ECDSA signatures in Bitcoin are DER-encoded, so they vary in size and can reach 72 bytes; BIP 340 uses a simple fixed format instead. Public keys shrink from the usual 33-byte compressed point to 32 bytes, because only the x coordinate is kept.

blocks.title: Fixed sizes, smaller keys
blocks.caption: One byte ruler. A DER signature’s size depends on its values; a BIP 340 signature never changes size, and a key keeps only the x coordinate of its compressed form.

blocks.text: Consensus requires verifiers to agree about which signatures are valid. BIP 340’s authors therefore specify verification at the byte level, including each rejection condition. They cite Bitcoin’s earlier problems with loosely specified DER parsing. An implementation cannot choose different checks and still follow this specification.

The first 32 bytes, *r*, encode the x coordinate of a curve point R chosen by the signer. The remaining 32 bytes encode a number, *s*. Verification checks the equation s⋅G = R + e⋅P. Here G is the curve’s fixed base point and P is the public key’s point. The challenge e is a hash that binds R, the public key and the message.

blocks.title: The equation a signature satisfies
blocks.caption: For vector 1 the two sides balance. Each term comes from the inputs, from the challenge hash, or from the curve’s fixed point G; Verify rearranges the equation to compute R.

blocks.text: Verification starts by converting the public key into a curve point. The function *lift_x* reads the key’s 32 bytes as an x coordinate. It returns the point with that x coordinate and an even y coordinate. It fails if x is too large or no such point exists. The verifier then reads r and s from the signature. It rejects r at or above the field size *p*, and s at or above the curve order *n*.

Next, compute the challenge e from a tagged hash of r, the public key and the message, reduced modulo n. Use it to compute R = s⋅G − e⋅P. Reject the signature if R is the point at infinity, its y coordinate is odd, or its x coordinate differs from r. Accept it only if every check passes.

Choose a valid vector below, then switch to an invalid one. The verifier stops at the first failure. A key with no curve point fails before hashing; a later failure means the inputs passed those earlier checks.

blocks.title: Verify, gate by gate
blocks.caption: Twelve published vectors, three valid and nine invalid. On a valid vector, swapping in another fixture’s message keeps the key and signature but changes e, so the recomputed R no longer fits.

blocks.text: Try the verifier’s message control on a valid vector. The key and signature stay the same, but another message changes e, which changes R. For every valid vector in the figure, that is enough to fail, at either the even-y check or the x comparison. Nothing in the verifier knows which message was “meant”; it only checks the one it is given.

blocks.title: Compare where the failures occur
blocks.caption: Each row follows a different published vector. The cross marks the first failed check; later checks are never reached.

blocks.summary: Why a vector’s comment can differ from its failure stage

blocks.text: Each vector in the CSV carries a short comment. These describe how a failing vector was built, not necessarily which check catches it. Vector 7 is labelled “negated message”, yet it never reaches the comparison of x(R) with r: the R it produces has an odd y coordinate, so it fails one step earlier. Vectors 8 and 11 do reach that comparison, and fail there. Reading the BIP’s algorithm and watching it run are two different kinds of evidence, and this page shows both.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: The figures show computed values and checks instead of a smooth curve. Points on secp256k1 use integer coordinates modulo a 256-bit prime. A textbook curve drawn over the real numbers would not represent those coordinates.

The challenge e is where the message enters. BIP 340 hashes it with a *tagged hash*: SHA-256 of the tag’s own SHA-256 written twice, followed by the data. Here the tag is the text BIP0340/challenge. The authors use tags so that a hash computed for one purpose cannot be reinterpreted as a hash for another.

The data is r, then the public key, then the message. Including the key is called key prefixing, and the authors explain why it matters. Without it, anyone could turn a valid signature for a key P into a valid signature for P + a⋅G, for any tweak a they like. They note this would make signatures insecure for keys made by adding tweaks, as BIP 32’s unhardened derivation and Taproot both do.

The message is hashed whole, whatever its length. Earlier revisions of BIP 340 required exactly 32 bytes, and the changelog records the lifting of that rule in April 2023. The published vectors include valid signatures over messages of 0, 1, 17 and 100 bytes alongside the usual 32. The BIP still recommends pre-hashing large messages for performance, and BIP 341’s transaction signatures do sign a 32-byte digest.

blocks.title: One hash, any message
blocks.caption: The challenge input for five valid vectors, to scale: 128 fixed bytes, then the message. A longer message only lengthens the tail.

blocks.summary: Details: why the signature carries R and not e

blocks.text: Schnorr signatures come in two forms. One publishes e and s; the other publishes R and s. BIP 340 chose R, which the authors say supports batch verification because no curve operation sits inside a hash. Batch verification checks many signatures together: it always succeeds if every signature is valid, and succeeds with only negligible probability if any is not.

Every valid x coordinate on the curve has two possible y values, one even and one odd. BIP 340 removes the ambiguity by rule: the key’s point P and the signature’s point R are always taken to have even y. That is why an x-only key is equivalent to a compressed key beginning with the byte 0x02.

The figure below shows the consequence in two places. The verifier lifts the key to its even-y point before anything else, and it rejects any R whose y turns out odd. The authors argue that, although it halves the set of valid public keys, it is not a reduction in security: breaking an x-only key is at most a small constant faster than breaking a full one. One side effect is stated outright: every public key has two matching secret keys, sk and n − sk.

blocks.title: One x, two y, one kept
blocks.caption: The even y is kept for the key and required of R: vector 6’s R has odd y, so Verify rejects it. The two secret keys are drawn without values.

blocks.text: lift_x fails if x ≥ p. Otherwise it computes c = x³ + 7 mod p and y = c^((p+1)/4) mod p, fails if y² ≠ c, and returns the point with whichever of y and p − y is even. The field size p and the curve order n are fixed 256-bit constants; the curve is y² = x³ + 7 over the integers modulo p.

sections.heading: What a passing check does not say

blocks.text: Successful verification means that the signature is valid for this public key and message under BIP 340. It does not establish what the message means. BIP 340 says applications should ensure that a message signed for one context is never accepted in a different context. For example, a signed application message should not be accepted as a transaction. The authors also explain that Schnorr signatures are non-malleable under their security assumptions, while ECDSA signatures are inherently malleable.

Nor does BIP 340 by itself provide a multisignature protocol. The key may belong to one person or be an aggregate of several. Schemes such as MuSig2, specified separately in BIP 327, let several parties build one key and one signature through an interactive protocol; to a verifier the result looks like any other signature. BIP 340 warns that multisignature schemes are generally insecure with the nonce generation of its default signing algorithm, or with any other deterministic method.

blocks.summary: Signing algorithms and the reference implementation

blocks.text: BIP 340 was assigned in 2020 and is recorded as deployed. This page explains the signing handoff but does not implement a signer. The BIP specifies a default signer, but signatures are not unique: other ways of generating its random value produce different, equally valid signatures, and however that value is generated, it must be uniformly random and not even partially predictable to an attacker. Verification is guaranteed to accept what a correct signer produces. The BIP’s own Python code is labelled for demonstration only; the values here come from the audited @noble/curves library, checked against all 19 vectors in the CSV.
